headline: Republican candidates keep some distance from Trump

sources.title: Most Republicans in tight midterm races distance themselves from Trump, Reuters review finds (Reuters, via Investing.com)
Voters favor Democrats on key issues but lack faith in either party to solve problems: AP-NORC poll (AP)
Republicans seek distance from Trump as US midterms loom (AFP, via The Standard)

chunks.text: On October 7, 2026, the news agency Reuters published a review of Republican candidates running for Congress. It found that candidates in 41 of 62 [[competitive races]] were {{backing away from}} President Donald Trump. Some have {{broken with}} him on at least one policy. Others have {{played down}} their [[ties]] to him. The vote on November 3 will decide which party controls Congress. The result could affect Trump's ability to {{carry out}} his [[agenda]].

verbs.correct: To keep some distance from someone
verbs.wrong: To ask a leader to visit your state
verbs.why: The mayor backed away from her old business partner after the scandal. Many fans backed away from the singer after his rude comments. Candidates in 41 of 62 competitive races were backing away from President Trump in some way.

verbs.correct: To publicly disagree with a leader
verbs.wrong: To choose a party's new leader
verbs.why: The senator broke with his party on the tax bill. Two members broke with the club's president on the vote. Some Republican candidates have broken with Trump on at least one policy.

verbs.correct: To make something seem less important
verbs.wrong: To make something easy to understand
verbs.why: The coach played down the injury to his star player. She played down her own role in the project. Some candidates have played down their ties to Trump.

verbs.correct: To do what you have planned
verbs.wrong: To explain a plan to voters
verbs.why: The city will carry out its new bus plan next year. The workers carried out the repairs in one day. The election result could affect Trump's ability to carry out his agenda.

chunks.text: Policy [[disagreements]] were the most common kind of split. They appeared in 23 of the 62 races, on issues such as [[beef imports]] and [[data centers]]. About a dozen candidates {{took down}} Trump's name, picture or [[endorsement]] from their websites. Most did this after winning their party's [[primary]]. Others {{stayed away from}} his events. Very few have {{spoken out against}} him directly. Most splits are over single issues, not his wider agenda.

verbs.correct: To remove something from a website
verbs.wrong: To check facts on a website
verbs.why: She took down the post after an hour. The store took down the old prices from its website. About a dozen candidates took down Trump's name, picture or endorsement from their campaign websites.

verbs.correct: To choose not to attend something
verbs.wrong: To give a speech at an event
verbs.why: Many workers stayed away from the meeting. She stayed away from the party because she was tired. Some candidates stayed away from Trump's events.

verbs.wrong: To repeat someone's words in a speech
verbs.why: Several nurses spoke out against the hospital's director. Two players spoke out against their coach after the game. Very few Republican candidates have spoken out against Trump directly.

chunks.text: Reuters says keeping distance from the president is not new. Democratic candidates did the same in 2014 and 2022. A Reuters poll put Trump's [[approval rating]] at 32 percent, the lowest of his career. In that poll, Republicans {{fell behind}} Democrats among [[registered voters]], 37 percent to 44 percent. Campaign advisers privately told Reuters that candidates need this distance to {{win over}} [[independent voters]].

verbs.correct: To have less support than a rival
verbs.wrong: To demand a new count of votes
verbs.why: The mayor fell behind her rival in the latest poll. Our candidate fell behind after the second debate. In a Reuters poll, Republicans fell behind Democrats among registered voters.

verbs.correct: To persuade someone to support you
verbs.wrong: To ask someone to answer a poll
verbs.why: The new teacher won over the class with her kindness. The small shop won over customers with friendly service. Advisers say candidates need distance from Trump to win over independent voters.

chunks.text: A Republican [[consultant]] {{summed up}} the challenge. She said candidates want [[credit]] for the government's successes without being tied too closely to the Trump [[brand]]. A White House spokesman {{stood by}} the president and called him the party's best messenger. An Associated Press poll in late September found that voters favor Democrats on the [[cost of living]], 38 percent to 27 percent. Few voters in that poll said either party can solve big problems. Republicans hope to {{hold on to}} control of Congress.

verbs.why: Can you sum up the movie in one sentence? The teacher summed up the lesson at the end of class. A Republican consultant summed up the challenge that candidates face.
Her friends stood by her during the trial. The fans stood by the team after many losses. A White House spokesman stood by Trump and called him the party's best messenger.

verbs.correct: To keep something you already have
verbs.wrong: To change the rules of something
verbs.why: The team held on to its lead until the final minute. She held on to her job when others lost theirs. Republicans hope to hold on to control of Congress.

vocab.def: To keep some distance from someone
ex: The company backed away from its partner when sales dropped.
Some voters backed away from the mayor after the news came out.
He backed away from his old friends after high school.

vocab.def: To publicly disagree with a leader
ex: The governor broke with her party on school funding.
He broke with his boss on the new rules.
A few members broke with the leader on the budget.

vocab.def: To make something seem less important
ex: The company played down the problem with its new phone.
He played down his success and thanked his team.
Officials played down the risk of more storms.

vocab.def: To do what you have planned
ex: The new mayor wants to carry out her plans quickly.
It took two years to carry out the changes.
The team carried out the plan without any problems.

vocab.def: To remove something from a website
ex: The school took down the photo after parents complained.
He took down his old videos last year.
The website took down the false story.

vocab.def: To choose not to attend something
ex: Many workers stayed away from the office party.
She stayed away from the meeting because she was sick.
Fans stayed away from the game after ticket prices rose.
Several workers spoke out against their manager at the meeting.
Some senators spoke out against the governor on TV.
A few parents spoke out against the principal.

vocab.def: To have less support than a rival
ex: The young candidate fell behind in the polls in October.
Her party fell behind its rivals in the big cities.
The senator fell behind his rival after the debate.

vocab.def: To persuade someone to support you
ex: She won over her neighbors by helping with their gardens.
The company won over young buyers with lower prices.
He gave a short speech and won over the crowd.
Let me sum up the main points of the report.
She summed up her vacation in three words.
The coach summed up the season in a short speech.
His wife stood by him when he lost his job.
The team stood by its coach after a bad season.
Most of his friends stood by him after the mistake.

vocab.def: To keep something you already have
ex: The champion held on to her title for three years.
The party held on to the governor's office in the last election.
He worked hard to hold on to his best customers.

wordDefs.def: Elections where both sides have a real chance to win
ex: Both parties spend a lot of money in competitive races.
There are only a few competitive races in our state this year.
Competitive races often bring more people out to vote.

wordDefs.def: Links or connections between people or groups
ex: The two countries have close ties.
She cut her ties with the company after she left.
The mayor has strong ties to local business owners.

wordDefs.def: A list of things a leader or group plans to do
ex: The new mayor has a busy agenda for her first year.
Lower taxes are at the top of his agenda.
The union shared its agenda with the company.

wordDefs.def: Times when people do not have the same opinion
ex: My brother and I have small disagreements about money.
The team settled its disagreements before the game.
There were many disagreements at the town meeting.

wordDefs.def: Beef that one country buys from other countries
ex: Beef imports rose when local prices went up.
Some farmers worry that beef imports will lower their prices.
The country limited beef imports after a disease outbreak.

wordDefs.def: Large buildings full of computers that store and process information
ex: Data centers use a lot of electricity.
Two new data centers are being built near the river.
Many tech companies are building data centers in Texas.

wordDefs.def: Public support for a person, especially in an election
ex: The candidate got an endorsement from the local newspaper.
Her endorsement helped him win the race.
The union gave its endorsement to the mayor.

wordDefs.def: An election that chooses a party's candidate
ex: She won the primary by a few hundred votes.
Only party members can vote in that primary.
The primary will take place in June.

wordDefs.def: The share of people who say a leader is doing a good job
ex: The governor's approval rating rose after the storm.
A low approval rating can hurt a leader's party.
Her approval rating is higher in rural areas.

wordDefs.def: People who have signed up officially so they can vote
ex: The city has about two million registered voters.
Only registered voters can take part in the election.
More young people became registered voters this year.

wordDefs.def: Voters who do not belong to any political party
ex: Independent voters often decide close elections.
Both candidates are trying to reach independent voters.
Many independent voters care most about prices.

wordDefs.def: An expert who is paid to give advice
ex: The school hired a consultant to plan its budget.
My aunt works as a consultant for small businesses.
The consultant said the company should cut costs.

wordDefs.def: Praise or thanks for something good that someone did
ex: She deserves credit for the team's success.
He took credit for an idea that was not his.
The workers got no credit for their extra hours.

wordDefs.def: The image and reputation people connect with a name
ex: The singer built her brand on social media.
A bad review can hurt a company's brand.
His personal brand is about hard work and honesty.

wordDefs.def: The amount of money people need for basic things like food and rent
ex: The cost of living is very high in New York.
Many families moved because of the rising cost of living.
Our pay did not keep pace with the cost of living.

mainIdea.s: A Reuters review found that most Republicans in close congressional races are keeping some distance from the president. Many hope this will help them gain independent voters in November.
mainIdea.why: Candidates in 41 of 62 competitive races were backing away from the president. Advisers say this distance helps them win over independent voters.

mainIdea.s: Most Republicans in close races have openly rejected the president on his main plans. They now criticize him at every rally, hoping this will earn them the support of many angry voters.
mainIdea.why: Close, but most splits are over single issues, not his wider agenda. Very few candidates have spoken out against the president directly.

mainIdea.s: A new study shows that fewer young Americans expect to cast ballots in the midterm elections. Researchers say many feel that neither political party cares about their worries over rent and jobs.
mainIdea.why: This story is about Republican candidates keeping some distance from the president. Some have broken with him on policy, and others have played down their ties.

tf.s: Candidates in 41 of 62 competitive races were backing away from Trump.
tf.why: The Reuters review found this in 41 of the 62 races before the November 3 elections.

tf.s: Most of the candidates who took down Trump's name did it before their primary.
tf.why: Most of the candidates who took down Trump's name, picture or endorsement did it after they won their primary.

tf.s: Policy disagreements appeared in all 62 of the competitive races.
tf.why: Candidates broke with Trump on policy in 23 of the 62 races, not in all of them.

tf.s: In a Reuters poll, Republicans fell behind Democrats.
tf.why: Among registered voters, Democrats had 44 percent and Republicans had 37 percent.

tf.s: A White House spokesman stood by the president.
tf.why: The spokesman stood by Trump and called him the party's best messenger.

tf.s: Most of the candidates have spoken out against Trump directly.
tf.why: Very few candidates have spoken out against him directly. Most splits are over single issues.

lines.text: Did you see the Reuters review of Republican candidates?
Most of the ones in close races are {{backing away from}} President Trump.
Some have {{broken with}} him on a policy, like beef imports. Others {{took down}} his picture from their websites.
So they're trying to [[play it safe]].
Right. A Republican consultant {{summed it up}} well. They want credit for the wins, but not the Trump brand.
Sounds like they want to [[have it both ways]].
Maybe. But very few have {{spoken out against}} him directly.
He's still very powerful in the party. They have to [[walk a fine line]].
Republicans {{fell behind}} Democrats in a Reuters poll.
So they need to {{win over}} independent voters.
Exactly. A lot of those voters are still [[on the fence]].
And what does the White House say?
A spokesman {{stood by}} the president. Republicans hope to {{hold on to}} Congress.
Well, it sounds like the candidates are trying to [[read the room]].

expressions.def: Used to say that someone avoids taking risks
ex: It might rain, so let's play it safe and bring a jacket.
She played it safe and kept her old job.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone wants two things that do not really go together
ex: You can't have it both ways. Either you save money or you buy the car.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone must be careful between two different risks
ex: Teachers walk a fine line between being kind and being strict.
The company walked a fine line with its new prices.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone has not decided yet
ex: I'm still on the fence about the new job.
Many shoppers are on the fence about electric cars.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone notices how other people feel and acts on it
ex: He didn't read the room and told a joke at the wrong time.
A good speaker knows how to read the room.
